Text at the top reads: The hose was cold, the shampoo was 'gentle,' and nobody warned me about the fly spray. I'm still the best-looking thing in this barn.
posts.caption: The wash rack is the one place on this farm where she loses every argument with me. I had a hose, a bucket, and forty-five minutes before the boarders arrived for the open house. She stood through shampoo, conditioner, and the little comb for her forelock without a single sigh, because a mirror was leaning against the tack trunk. The second the water shut off she shook like a wet dog and soaked my good jeans. Then she checked her reflection and approved. I spent the rest of the afternoon in a borrowed barn sweatshirt that said 'Hay Fever.' It fit.
posts.first: I keep a spare brush in the truck for days like that. She has never once thanked me for it. Last spring I braided her forelock, she held perfectly still for twelve minutes, and then she pulled it out on the walk back to her stall. I braided it again. We have an understanding.

The carabiner is now on the ground in two pieces. I've ordered a different gate.
posts.first: The feed store sold me the strongest latch they carry, and the clerk asked what I was keeping in. I said one pony. He wrote up the receipt without another word. Pudding was out again by supper, waiting at the back door with a very polite face.

posts.quote: The mail carrier keeps a carrot in her truck now. She says she never agreed to this. The horse believes she agreed in March.
posts.first: The first time she stopped, it was only to hand over a package. He leaned over the fence and gently pulled the sleeve of her jacket. She laughed and went back to the truck for a banana. He ate the banana. After that, the carrot was just the natural next step.

posts.caption: The old boy walks the fence every morning at about the time the coffee finishes. He used to run it, ears pinned, kicking up mud and carrying on like a racehorse in a western. Now he walks it with his nose low, stopping at every post as if he's reading the news. Last week he spent ten minutes at the corner by the maple, where a family of chipmunks has built something he clearly approves of. I sat on the tailgate with my coffee and let him take his time. Nobody on this farm is in a hurry anymore.
posts.first: He's twenty-nine this spring. The vet says his joints are fine for his age, which is the nicest thing anyone has said about mine, too. I've started walking the fence with him in the mornings. He doesn't speed up for me. I wouldn't want him to.

posts.caption: The first load of second cutting came in at 3:30 and the hay guy had it stacked by 4:15. Before he'd even finished the last row, she was standing in the barn aisle with her nose in the air, not moving. I walked past her three times before I realized she wasn't waiting for anything. She was just breathing. The whole barn smelled like a summer afternoon, and the cat on her back hadn't opened an eye. I stood there for a minute too, then I went to the house and got a chair.
posts.first: The hay guy says this is the best second cutting he's baled in years. He said it twice, which for him is a speech. I carried a flake to her stall myself instead of using the wheelbarrow. She put her whole face in it and stayed there.

posts.caption: I should have known when the clippers came out of the drawer and the whole barn went quiet. Big Red heard that drawer open from the far end of the aisle. She walked into her stall, turned around, and filled the doorway like a closed gate. I held the clippers and she held a look. The farrier, who was there for her feet, put his tools down and said he'd come back later. I trimmed one ear, very carefully, while she watched me in the aisle mirror. The whiskers are staying. That's the settlement.
posts.first: I've groomed this mare for nine years and I know exactly where the line is. It's about an inch from her lip. Last winter I crossed it once with a pair of scissors and I still hear about it. She's very patient with everything except surprises that have a motor.
